newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU reject most science fears on gene-maize.
newsitem.headline: EU reject most science fears on gene-maize.

text.p: The following are some of the arguments raised for and against market approval of Ciba Geigy's gene-modified maize, which the European Commission cleared for release on Wednesday.
The strain was approved by U.S. authorities for cultivation in this year's harvest in the United States.
Swiss chemical company Ciba-Geigy developed its maize to be resistant to the herbicide glufosinate, commonly marketed as Basta, and to carry the Bt-toxin to repel corn-borer pests.

Environmental and consumer groups have said the release of glufosinate-resistant species into the environment raises the possibility of cross-breeding with wild, weed varieties which will then be more difficult to control.

They also say glufosinate resistance in plants could mean farmers take less care in applying the powerful weedkiller, leading to greater releases of its breakdown products into water courses and from there into drinking water supplies.
The European Commission said on Wednesday the weedkiller would not be allowed for use on Ciba's genetically modified strain for the moment.

"The impact on human health and the environment from the use of the herbicide gluphosinate ammonimum on the genetically modified maize lines will be assessed under Directive 91/414/EEC on plant protection products before authorization is given for the use of this herbicide on Bt-maize," a statement said.
Environmentalists say that building the Bt-toxin directly into plant species will greatly increase insect resistance to the toxin itself, which is already used as a low-impact pesticide.

"A potential development of insect resistance to the Bt-toxin cannot be considered an adverse environmental effect, as existing agricultural means of controlling such resistant species of insects will be available," the Commission said.

Not so, according to the environmental group Greenpeace, which said in a Wednesday news release: "The Commission's ignorance about the value of organic farming and sustainable agriculture is revealed in (this) statement."
The Bt-maize strain also carries an antibiotic "marker gene", used to show that a seed has taken up the genetic changes desired by the biotechnologists but redundant once that step is complete.
Fears raised by opponents of approval concern the effect of the modified corn's release on bacterial resistance to the Ampicillin antibiotic, which they say should and can be removed.

The Commission did not answer this question directly on Wednesday but did say: "There is no reason to believe that the genetic modification of Bt-maize will give rise to any adverse affects on human health from its use in human food."
It repeated the same formulation for the effects on livestock by substituting the word "animal" for "human". -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
